Prop Edge Engine · NFL 2026 · Week 4

Week 4 Picks

Paper picks, logged before kickoff and scored Monday. The model has not yet shown it can beat the book in Week 1, so every pick here is an argument, not a promise. This is analysis, not advice.

Built Sun Oct 4, 10:01 am PDT from DraftKings odds captured 2026-10-04 at 09:55 ET. Next update: Friday Sep 11 evening, after the 4 pm ET injury report (Week 1 practice reports start Wed Sep 9). How the picks are made.

How to read this page
Paper picks. This sheet covers the 1 pm, 4 pm and Sunday night games and Monday night only: it was written after the early kickoffs and the London game, which are not covered. Three weeks in, the book has been closer than the model on every week's rungs; the engine's favorable calls have hit 44, 51 and 54 in 100 against prices near 50. No leg on today's late slate clears the Play rule with usage that fits, so everything here is a Lean. Candidates are shown with three weeks of usage as information; only players who are out or whose quarterback changed were removed. Logged before kickoff, scored Tuesday.

Three views. Picks is the sheet: the legs worth a bet, each with its price, the chance the price implies and the chance the model gives it. Games has one card per game in DraftKings order: kickoff, venue, roof, total, spread, the kickoff forecast, the verdict, the pick and its checks, the book's main lines and the players the model covers. All odds is every ladder the book listed, every rung, beside the model's chance.

Verdicts. Play means we would bet it: our number says it hits more often than the price suggests, the player did it often enough last year to back that up, and the defense he faces does not argue against it. A Play also has to keep at least 10 points of edge in the worst case, meaning if the opposing defense repeats last season in full (the Sensitivity line on each pick). Lean means we like it but something real gets in the way, so we are not betting it and it stays out of parlays; if you bet it anyway, bet small. Pass means the price is fair or too short, so there is no bet.

Parlays. Legs in different games multiply exactly, so the slip price is the product of the leg prices. For legs in the same game DraftKings reprices for correlation, and the displayed price will be lower than the product shown.

Weather. Each card shows the roof and the kickoff-hour forecast: weather.gov when its hourly forecast reaches the kickoff (about 6.5 days out), Open-Meteo before that, each labelled with the source. Rain enters the model as a chance shared by everyone in the game; wind of 15 mph or more shortens the passing game; indoor games carry no weather term.

Players tables. QB is the passer expected to start ("new" marks a change from last season, which the model discounts). Role is the share of the team's pass plays the receiver ran a route on last season, plus expected carries for backs; it is the volume input the model uses. Snap percent is for reference.

Top

The picks

Book says is how often the price says it should hit. Model says is how often we think it hits. When ours is higher, that gap is the whole reason to bet. Odds are DraftKings prices at capture and move.

Every leg carries its reasons as bullets. Singles first, then the same-game pairs that only make sense together.

Longer parlays across bet types (lottery tickets)

Cross-game slips built from the best-value leg in each game across every market, one leg per game, so the price is exactly the product of the legs. A leg qualifies only if it clears the model's 3-point bar in the 35% to 75% book band, is not a mover, carries no new-quarterback or teammate-absence flag, was not rejected in this week's review, and the player's own record last season at that rung is at least what the price asks. Every added leg multiplies both the payout and the chance of losing; these hit a few times a season at best.

The achievable sheet

The other way to read the same numbers: for each player, the surest bet whose price is still favorable, not the biggest gap. How the picks are made

Each game is simulated thousands of times as one offense: the play count, the split between dropbacks and runs, every receiver's targets, catches and yards, every back's carries and yards, and the quarterback's passing line as the sum of what his receivers do plus the throws to everyone else. A quarterback's passing yards and his receiver's yards are therefore priced together, and a back's carries fall in the same simulated games where the passing volume rises.

Behind that sit every receiver's route share, target rate, depth of target, catch rate and yards per catch, both teams' tempo, the total and spread, venue, kickoff window and forecast. The opposing defense enters as five measured terms (yards per target, catch rate, passing touchdowns per attempt, yards per carry and rushing touchdowns per carry allowed, each relative to the league and shrunk hard because defense barely repeats year to year) plus the total and spread. Teammates share the game's pass volume, so paired legs are priced together. A leg makes the list only when the model's number beats the price by a clear margin, the player's own record supports it, and a plain-language reason survives. Games a teammate missed count at 30%, games under a different quarterback at 50%, deep rungs are excluded, and players on a new team are shown but never picked.
